title: Learned tutoring policies show different classroom learning and override patterns
summary: In a probability-tutor classroom study, an apprenticeship-learned policy overrode student choices less often than a conservative-Q-learning policy (28.2% versus 66.7% of recorded decisions). Among non-ceiling students, the apprenticeship group had a higher mean standard posttest score (.908 versus .842), with a marginal planned one-sided pretest-adjusted contrast. Small samples, repeated decisions and an augmented historical control limit broader superiority claims.
ai_technology: StuEDM; energy-based distribution matching; conservative Q-learning

source_review.scope: Original v1 dissertation front, authorship/version distinctions and Chapter 7 learned-policy Methods, classroom design, Results and limitations

evidence.tested: StuEDM was trained on 244 earlier student trajectories; StuCQL used 2,716. The Spring 2026 live study had 104 completers. Removing perfect-pretest students left 26 StuEDM and 27 StuCQL students; the random-mode Expert comparator was augmented with 11 prior-semester students. Table 7.1 reports a planned one-sided adjusted contrast p=.048 for StuEDM versus StuCQL; the three-group omnibus test was not significant.
evidence.unknown: The Expert arm is partly historical, and non-significant baseline tests do not prove population equivalence. Other direct learning comparisons against StuCQL were not significant. Multiple directional outcomes, ceiling exclusions, a single course and small samples limit inference. Override counts include repeated decisions within students; decision-level significance is not independent-person replication. Longer tutor time is measured engagement, not proof of benefit. Earlier dissertation chapters reproduce published methods, which are not represented as new here; October 20 is the located arXiv version date, not a claim of absolute first circulation.
evidence.ai_role: An energy-based neural policy learned from student demonstration occupancy selects presentation modes and overrides conflicting choices during new classroom use; measured learning and choice patterns are the represented field result. Formatting assistance by a separate language model is unrelated to this contribution.
